A specially appointed judge ruled in favor of Apple in the company's effort to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies to help defend itself against the Justice Department's antitrust lawsuit. Here's what happened.

Background

Last May, Apple asked the court overseeing the Justice Department's 2024 antitrust case against it to force the following 14 federal agencies to hand over documents related to their evaluation, purchase, and use of smartphones and wearable devices:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

Apple argued in its motion that those records could support its defense against allegations that its iPhone policies were anticompetitive.

In short, Apple's theory was that if federal agencies chose its products for reasons related to security, privacy, or other features, that would support the company's argument that the contested practices are legitimate product advantages rather than anticompetitive restrictions.

The government pushed back, arguing that the agencies had nothing to do with the case, didn't regulate smartphones, and didn't purchase or use these products the way typical consumers did.

It asked the court to quash the subpoenas, saying what they sought was irrelevant and an undue burden, and could include privileged, confidential, or national-security-sensitive material.

The court then referred the dispute to retired federal judge Jose Linares, who is serving as a special discovery master to decide whether Apple can enforce the subpoenas.

In complex cases involving extensive discovery, courts sometimes appoint a special master to handle narrower disputes and ease the load on the presiding judge. Special masters can be retired judges, practicing lawyers, or other experts with relevant experience.

Apple wins right to obtain documents from federal agencies

Judge Linares has now ruled for Apple, finding that all of its document requests are relevant to the core allegations in the case. He also said the government hadn't sufficiently supported its broader objections.

Even though the special discovery master sided with Apple, that doesn't mean the company will immediately get all the documents it requested.

Instead, the agencies can still withhold specific records they consider privileged or otherwise protected, but they have to list each one in a privilege log. Any disputes over those claims could spark another round of discovery fights, potentially including private review by Judge Linares.
